When we got back to the raft, he counted the money and found he'd collected eighty-seven dollars and seventy-five cents. He'd also brought a three-gallon jug of whisky that he found beneath a wagon as he started home through the woods. The king said that, taken altogether, it beat any day he'd ever spent in the missionary business. There was no arguing with it, he said: heathens couldn't compare with pirates when it came to working a camp meeting.

The duke had thought he'd done pretty well until the king showed up, but afterward he wasn't so impressed with himself. At the printing office he'd set and printed two small orders for farmers, advertisements for horses, and pocketed four dollars. He'd also obtained ten dollars' worth of advertisements for the newspaper by offering to print them for four dollars if they paid in advance. They had. A year's subscription normally cost two dollars, but he sold three for fifty cents each, provided they paid him immediately. They'd intended to pay with firewood and onions as usual, but he explained that he had just bought the business, lowered the price as far as possible, and would now accept only cash. He composed a little poem entirely out of his own head, three rather sweet and sorrowful verses called 'Yes, Crush, Cold World, This Breaking Heart.' He left it typeset and ready for the paper without charging anything. In all, he collected nine dollars and fifty cents and said he'd put in a fairly honest day's work for it.

Then he showed us another free printing job, this one for our benefit. It pictured an escaped Black slave carrying a bundle on a stick over his shoulder, with '$200 reward' printed beneath. The text concerned Jim and described him exactly. It claimed he'd escaped from St. Jacques' plantation, forty miles below New Orleans, the previous winter and probably headed north. Anyone who captured and returned him would receive the reward plus expenses.

'Now,' the duke said, 'after tonight we can travel by daylight whenever we want. If we see anyone approaching, we can bind Jim's hands and feet with rope, lay him in the shelter, show this notice, and say we caught him upriver. We'll explain that we couldn't afford a steamboat, so our friends let us have this little raft on credit, and we're heading down to collect the reward.'

They passed deserted brickfields. The fog thinned here, revealing strange bottle-shaped kilns with orange tongues of flame spreading like fans. A dog barked as they went by, and somewhere far off in the darkness a stray gull screamed. The horse caught a hoof in a rut, swerved, and broke into a gallop.

Eventually they left the clay road and rattled once more over roughly paved streets. Most windows were dark, though here and there bizarre shadows appeared against a lamplit blind. He studied them with curiosity. They moved like monstrous puppets, gesturing like living creatures. He hated them. A heavy anger filled his heart. As they rounded a corner, a woman shouted something from an open doorway. Two men chased the hansom for about a hundred yards, and the driver lashed at them with his whip.

People say that passion makes the mind go round in circles. Certainly Dorian Gray's bitten lips repeated those subtle phrases about soul and sensation with a dreadful persistence, until they seemed to express his mood completely. By approving them intellectually, he justified impulses that would have governed him even without justification. The same thought crept from cell to cell within his brain. The fierce desire to live, most terrifying of human appetites, sent energy through every trembling nerve and fibre. Ugliness, once hateful because it made things real, now attracted him for exactly that reason. It was the only reality. The vulgar quarrel, the disgusting den, the brutal violence of chaotic lives, the sheer degradation of thieves and outcasts—all impressed themselves upon him more vividly than art's graceful forms or music's dreamlike shadows. These were what he needed to forget. In three days he would be free.

Suddenly the driver stopped sharply at the entrance to a dark lane. Above the low roofs and uneven chimney stacks rose the black masts of ships, their yards wrapped in white mist like spectral sails.

'Somewhere around here, isn't it, sir?' he asked hoarsely through the hatch.

Dorian started and looked about. 'This will do,' he answered. He climbed down quickly, paid the extra fare he had promised, and hurried toward the quay. Here and there a lantern glimmered at the stern of a great merchant ship. Its light trembled and broke apart in the puddles. A steamer loading coal before departure gave off a red glow. The slippery pavement looked like a wet waterproof coat.

Mrs Musgrove seized the first chance to speak with Anne privately. 'Oh, Miss Anne, I do wish Mrs Charles possessed something of your way with the children. With you they are entirely different creatures! Generally, of course, they are sadly spoilt. What a pity you cannot teach your sister to manage them. Such fine, healthy little children, poor dears—no partiality in saying so! Yet Mrs Charles has no notion how to treat them. Good heavens, what a nuisance they can be! I assure you, Miss Anne, it makes me less eager to have them at our house than I would otherwise be. Mrs Charles, I think, is rather displeased that I do not invite them more frequently. But children are a trial when one must constantly correct them: don't touch this, don't do that; or purchase tolerable behaviour with more cake than is wholesome.'

Mary also confided in her. 'Mrs Musgrove believes her servants so dependable that questioning it would amount to treason. Yet, without any exaggeration, I am certain that her senior housemaid and laundry maid spend all day roaming the village instead of attending to their work. Wherever I go, there they are. I declare I cannot visit the nursery twice without finding some sign of them. If Jemima were not the most reliable, steady creature alive, they would corrupt her completely; she tells me they are forever urging her to walk out with them.' Mrs Musgrove's account, meanwhile, ran thus: 'I never interfere with my daughter-in-law's arrangements; I know too well that it would not answer. But I shall mention this to you, Miss Anne, since you may be able to remedy matters. I have little confidence in Mrs Charles's nursery maid. Strange tales reach me about her, and she is always off gadding. I can say from personal knowledge that she dresses so extravagantly as to ruin any servant who associates with her. Mrs Charles puts absolute faith in her, I know. Still, I offer this hint so you may keep an eye open. Should you notice anything wrong, you need not hesitate to speak.'

Then Mary complained that, when other families dined with them at the Great House, Mrs Musgrove frequently neglected to accord her the precedence she deserved. Why, she asked, should being regarded as one of the household deprive her of her proper place?
